title.en: Tamus, Pupal, and the Coconut-Shell Oracle
title.zh: 塔穆斯、帕帕與椰殼神諭

region.en: Sulka country, northern New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛北部蘇爾卡人之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Abandoned because she was pregnant while a cannibal couple ravaged the land, Tamus bore a son who turned a dracaena plant into a companion, Pupal. The two boys slew the cannibals and sent the ogress's breasts afloat in a coconut shell as an oracle that sank only when the fugitives spoke the truth.
summary.zh: 食人夫婦肆虐，村人棄孕婦塔穆斯而逃。她產下一子，其子以龍血樹造出同伴帕帕。二童築滑障、練武藝，誘食人者前來而誅之；塔穆斯將母食人妖之乳裝入椰殼放流，設下神諭：若流亡者撒謊則浮，說真話則沉。村民依諭而返，二童先拒其登岸，以棄母之罪責之，後宥之，眾人重聚故里。

passages.text: Once there was a cannibal and his wife who had killed and eaten a great many persons, so that, fearing lest they should all be destroyed, the people resolved to abandon their village and seek safety in flight. But Tamus, one of the women of the village, was with child, whence the others refused to take her with them; she swam after them, however, and clung to the stern of one of the canoes, but they beat her off, compelling her to return to the deserted village and to live there alone. In due time she bore a son, and warned him never to talk or laugh, lest the cannibals should hear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day his mother left him a dracaena-plant as a plaything, and when she was gone he said to himself, 'What shall I make out of this, my brother or my cousin?' Then he held the dracaena behind him, and presently it turned into a boy, with whom he played and talked — Pupal, hidden behind a partition in the house. When their mother discovered the companion, the two boys reassured her: 'Have no fear; we shall kill them, if they dare to come.' Making shields and spears, practising marksmanship, and raising a slippery barricade, they set up a swing near the house and called out, 'Where are you? We are here, come and eat us.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the cannibals tried to climb the barricade, they slipped and fell, and the boys rushing out succeeded in killing them both after a hard fight. Tamus cut up the bodies and burned them, saving only the breasts of the ogress, which she put in a coco-nut-shell and set afloat on the sea: 'Go to the people who ran away from here, and if they ask, Have the cannibals killed Tamus? — remain floating; but if they say, Has Tamus borne a son and has he killed the cannibals? — then sink!' All occurred as Tamus had foreseen, and through the aid of the coco-nut-shell the people learned the truth. When the fugitives set out for their old home, Pupal and Tamus's son attacked them, saying, 'Ye abandoned my mother and cast her away. Now, ye shall not come back'; but after a while he relented and allowed the people to land, and all lived together again happily and safely in their old home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Twins of the Dead Mother Avenge Taso
title.zh: 亡母雙子誅食人者塔索

region.en: New Hebrides, Vanuatu (symbolic pin: Espíritu Santo)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖新赫布里底群島（象徵定位：聖靈島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The cannibal Taso killed Qatu's pregnant sister and left her body in a thicket, where twin boys were born of the dead woman. Reared by their uncle on sago-frond bows, they ripened a tabued banana bunch bottom-up as their victory sign, then crushed Taso with the hot stones of his own oven.
summary.zh: 食人者塔索殺害孕姊，棄屍灌叢；雙生子竟由亡母腹中誕生，以雨水嫩芽活命。舅父卡圖收養之，以西米葉小弓練其射技。長成後，二人在蕉樹上設禁：若蕉串自頂向下熟，即塔索殺我；自底向上熟，即我殺塔索。二人潛入塔索屋中之男子會所，以爐中熱石砸殺塔索，誅其母，焚屋而歸，舅父聞竹爆聲急往，途中遇之，知母仇已報。

passages.text: There was once a cannibal named Taso, who came one day upon the sister of Qatu and killed her, but did not eat her because she was with child. So he abandoned her body in a thicket, and there, though their mother was dead, twin boys were born. They found rain-water collected in dead leaves, and shoots of plants that they could eat; and when they grew old enough to walk, they wandered in the forest until one day they found a sow belonging to their uncle Qatu, eating its provisions daily until he caught them — and, hearing who they were, welcomed them as his nephews.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Qatu made little bows of sago fronds for them, and when they could shoot lizards, he broke the bows, giving them larger ones with which they brought down greater game; and thus he trained them until they were grown up and could shoot anything. When they were young men, Qatu told them about Taso and how he had murdered their mother. The twins determined to kill the cannibal, so they set a tabu on a banana-tree belonging to them and said to their uncle: 'If our bunch of bananas begins to ripen at the top and ripens downwards, you will know that Taso has killed us; but if it begins to ripen at the bottom and ripens upwards, we shall have killed him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came to his house, Taso had gone to the beach to sharpen his teeth, and only his mother was at home. The twins sat in the gamal, the men's house, roasting yams and heating stones in the blaze; and Taso's mother sang a song, telling him that there were two men in the gamal and that they should be food for him and for her. The cannibal quickly returned from the shore, moving his head from side to side and striking the trees so that they went crashing down. When he climbed over the door-rail of the gamal, the boys immediately threw at him all the hot rocks from the oven and knocked him down, and then with their clubs they beat him until he was dead, after which they killed his mother, and setting fire to the house over them, went away. Now Qatu, hearing the popping of the bamboos as the house burned, said, 'Alas, Taso has probably burned the boys!' Hastening to see what had happened, he met them on the way and heard from them that they had killed Taso and had revenged their mother whom he had slain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Brothers and the Cannibal Who Killed His Own House
title.zh: 四兄弟與自滅滿門之食人妖

region.en: Melanesia (tale of general distribution; symbolic pin: Solomon Islands)
region.zh: 美拉尼西亞通用故事（象徵定位：所羅門群島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Three brothers each answered a cannibal's challenge to 'call my brothers' by making buried fish reply, so the ogre let them take his breadfruit. The youngest, who had killed his fish outright, was trapped in the tree — but he talked the stupid monster into felling every tree he stood near, his own children, his wife, and last his own hand, before coming down and slaying him.
summary.zh: 長兄射魚埋沙，攀食人妖之麵包樹，妖令其呼弟為證，埋魚齊聲應之，妖懼而放行。二弟三弟效之皆得手。幼弟殺魚不埋，無魚應聲，被困樹上；他卻誘妖：『我將從那棵樹上下來』——妖連砍週遭樹木，又殺自己幼女、妻子，最後砍斷己手；男子下樹而誅之。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); tale of general Melanesian distribution.

passages.text: In a village lived four brothers, the eldest of whom one day took his bow and went out to shoot fish. Those which were only wounded he buried in the sand, and so went on until his arrow hit and stuck in the trunk of a bread-fruit-tree; whereupon, looking up and seeing ripe fruit, he climbed the tree and threw several of them down. An old cannibal heard the sound as they dropped and said, 'Who is that stealing my fruit?' The man in the tree replied, 'It is I with my brothers,' and the old ogre answered, 'Well, let us see if what you say is true. Just call to them.' Accordingly the man shouted, 'My brothers!' and all the fish that he had buried in the sand replied, so that it sounded as if many men were near; whereupon the cannibal was frightened and said, 'It is true, but hurry up, take what you will, only leave me the small ones.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The second brother followed his tracks and imitated his procedure and came back with fish and fruit; the third brother did the same. Then came the turn of the fourth, who failed to bury the wounded fish but killed them, and when the cannibal asked him to call his brothers, there was no reply. 'Aha,' said the cannibal, 'now I have got you. You must come down from the tree.' 'Oh, yes!' said the youngest brother, 'I shall come down on that tree there.' Quickly the ogre took his axe and cut down the tree, and in this way he felled every one that stood near. 'Now, I surely have you,' said he, but the youngest brother replied, 'No, I will come down on your youngest daughter there.' So the cannibal rushed at her and gave her a fatal blow; and thus the man in the tree induced the stupid monster to kill all his children and his wife and lastly to cut off his own hand, whereupon the man came down from the tree and slew the ogre.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Widower's Armbands and the Flooded Tree-Root

region.en: Melanesia (tale of general distribution; symbolic pin: Solomon Islands)
region.zh: 美拉尼西亞通用故事（象徵定位：所羅門群島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A cave-monster stole a household's stored food and walled wife and children alive in a cave. The widower mourned a year, then lured the cannibal to sleep on a tree-root in a dammed river-bed with the promise of plaited armlets; the birds broke the dam, and the flood drowned the monster while the man tore off his mourning bands.
summary.zh: 洞穴妖盜食藏糧，又將婦人與孩童封入洞中餓死。鰥夫居喪編臂環，妖羨而求之；他答：『須先睡，方能編得工整。』遂密令群鳥截流，引妖臥於乾河床之大樹根上，以藤索縛之；鳥決堤，洪水奔下。妖問『這涼物是什麼？』男子答曰：『你這惡洞妖，食物本是為我們備的，你吃光並害死我妻兒，如今還想要臂環？』遂撕下喪環擲地，洪水沒頂，妖溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Dixon notes close Indonesian parallels.

passages.text: A man and his family had dried and prepared a great quantity of food, which they stored on a staging in their home; and one day, when the man had gone off to his field to work, a cannibal came to the house. Seeing all the provisions, he resolved to get them. So he said to the man's wife, 'Your cousin told me to tell you to give me a package of food.' The woman gave him one, and he hid it in the forest, after which he returned and repeated his request, thus carrying away all the food which the people had stored. Finally he seized the woman and her children, shut them up in a cave, and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the husband returned, he found his house empty; his wife and family starved to death in the cave he could not open, and he returned to his town and plaited the widower's wristlets and arm-bands for himself. One day the old cannibal came by, and seeing him sitting there, admired the plaited ornaments and asked the man to make him some like them. The widower agreed: 'You must first go to sleep, then I can make them properly.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they went to seek a suitable place, and the man, after secretly telling the birds to dam up the river, led the cannibal to a great tree-root in the channel of the stream. Believing him, the cannibal lay down on the root and slept, whereupon the man took strong rattans and vines and tied the monster fast, after which he called out to the birds to break the dam and let the flood come down the river. When the cannibal, awakened by the water which rose higher and higher, cried out, 'What is this cold thing which touches me?' the man replied: 'You evil cave-monster, surely it was for you that we prepared all the food, and you came and ate it up. You also killed my wife and children, and now you want me to plait an arm-band for you.' Then he tore off his own arm-bands and signs of mourning and threw them away, while the water rose above the head of the cannibal and drowned him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.zh: 困於無花果樹之加拉瓦達

region.en: Melanesia (tale of general distribution; symbolic pin: Solomon Islands)
region.zh: 美拉尼西亞通用故事（象徵定位：所羅門群島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The witch mother-in-law imprisoned Garawada in a fig-tree by magic; her son was born and fell to the jungle floor, where he grew alone, fed his mother from below, and sang the identity song 'I have sucked the shoots of dabedabe; my mother is Garawada.' Rescued by his uncle's villagers, Garawada slipped free of the falling tree and turned into a crab.
summary.zh: 巫婆岳母施法夾困加拉瓦達於無花果樹杈間。她產子墜地，兒獨自長於叢林，採果奉母，並習唱認親歌：『我食過達貝達貝之嫩枝，吾母加拉瓦達也。』一日誤傷村童，其舅父出而認之，率眾伐樹救母；樹倒之際，加拉瓦達脫身奔至海灘，化為蟹，鑽入沙穴而去。兒隨舅返村，村童自此不再怕他。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); tale of general Melanesian distribution.

passages.text: A woman named Garawada one day went with her mother-in-law into the jungle to gather figs. Coming to a fig-tree, Garawada climbed up and began to eat the ripe fruit, while she threw down the green ones to her mother-in-law. The latter, angered at this, called to Garawada to come down, but when she reached the fork in the tree, the old woman, who was a witch, caused the forks to come together, thus imprisoning her daughter-in-law, after which she went away and left her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: For many days the woman remained in the tree, and finally bore a son; but after a while the child fell to the ground, and though his mother feared that he would die, he found wild fruits and water, and lived. One day he looked up into the tree and discovered his mother, and from that time he gave her fruits and berries in order that she might not starve. 'Mother, teach me my pari, that I may sing it when I find my people, and that thus they may know me' — and she taught him the spell: 'I have sucked the shoots of dabedabe; My mother is Garawada.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The child ran off to seek his way out of the jungle and came to the edge of the forest, where children threw darts at a rolled coco-nut; missing his aim, he struck one of the children in the arm, and all ran shrieking home. On the third visit the father of one of them ran out and caught him; the boy told his story and sang his song, and the man said, 'Truly thou art my nephew. Come, let us go and set thy mother free.' So they went with many of the villagers and cut down the tree; but as the tree fell, Garawada slipped away and ran swiftly to the beach, and there, turning into a crab, crawled into a hole in the sand. Her son wept because he knew that his mother had left him, but his uncle led him back to the village and took him into his own home, and the children no longer were afraid to have him for a playfellow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and the Winged Maiden of the Sky-Land

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Tagaro stole the wings of a bathing sky-maiden and married her; when her weeping over scolded yams wore the earth from her hidden wings, she flew back to heaven with her child. Tagaro built an arrow-chain to the sky and climbed a banian-root that crept down it — but halfway down his wife cut the root beneath her, and Tagaro fell to earth alone.
summary.zh: 塔加羅窺天女下凡沐浴，竊其翼藏於屋柱下，娶為妻。妻觸薯蔓而薯自熟，遭妯娌責罵，入屋倚柱而泣，淚滴蝕土露出雙翼，遂攜子飛回天上。塔加羅百箭連環射空成梯，天界榕根循箭而下，他攜飾物攀根而上尋妻；歸途夫妻相讓先下，行至半空，妻抽斧斷根，塔加羅與鳥墜地，妻與子重返天界。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Aoba heritage. Swan-maiden type, well developed in the New Hebrides.

passages.text: A party of heavenly, winged maidens once flew down to earth to bathe, and Tagaro watched them. He saw them take off their wings, stole one pair, and hid them at the foot of the main pillar of his house. He then returned and found all fled but the wingless one, and he took her to his house and presented her to his mother as his wife. After a time Tagaro took her to weed his garden, when the yams were not yet ripe, and as she weeded and touched the yam vines, ripe tubers came into her hand. Tagaro's brothers thought she was digging yams before their time and scolded her; she went into the house and sat weeping at the foot of the pillar, and as she wept her tears fell, and wearing away the earth pattered down upon her wings. She heard the sound, took up her wings, and flew back to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another version adds that the returning sky-maiden took her child with her; and Tagaro, finding the wings gone, knew that his wife and child had returned to the sky-land. He called a bird: 'Fly up and seek for them in their country, for you have wings and I have not.' The bird perched in the sky-country, scratched upon a fruit pictures of Tagaro, the child, and its mother, and dropped it at their feet. The sky-woman bade the bird tell Tagaro that he must ascend to the sky-land, for only if he should come up to her would she agree to descend to earth again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Quickly making a powerful bow and a hundred arrows, Tagaro shot one of them at the sky; it stuck firmly, and he shot another into the butt of the first, and a third into the butt of the second, making an arrow-chain until the end of it reached the earth. Then from the sky a banian-root crept down the arrow-chain and took root in the earth; Tagaro breathed upon it, and it grew larger and stronger, whereupon he and the bird climbed the banian-root to the sky. His wife gathered up her mats and followed him down; but when they were half way down, she took out a hatchet which she had concealed and cut the banian-root just beneath her, so that Tagaro and the bird fell to earth, while she and her child climbed back again to the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: Chasing a snared pigeon, a man came to an isle of women whose only husbands were tortoises. One woman saw him reflected in the spring and secreted him; discovered at last, he became husband to them all — until, homesick, he paddled home and his own wife, furious at the wasted funeral beads, felled him with an axe.
summary.zh: 男子追捕網中之鴿，遠航至女人之島——島上女子皆以龜為夫。一女在泉中窺見樹上男影，藉故折返留其日盾，密藏男子於家。事洩後眾女出資共聘之為夫。及其子長成，男子思鄉，解舟而歸；家人以為他已溺亡。夜叩鼓歸家，其妻舉火視之，怒斥：『你害我們白費葬禮珠錢，卻無恥地與別的女人過活！』舉斧擊之，男子遂死。

passages.text: A man one day set some snares in a tree to catch pigeons. One of the birds was caught, but succeeded in tearing the snare loose and flew away over the sea. The man, thinking to secure it, followed it in his canoe, and after having paddled all day and all night, in the morning he saw an island and the bird perched upon a tree. Concealing his canoe, he started after the bird, but hearing people coming, he hurriedly climbed into a tree and hid himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tree stood directly over a spring, and soon many women appeared, coming to get water. One of them, as she stooped to dip up water, saw the reflection of the man in the surface of the pool; whereupon she called out to her companions, 'I will fill your water-vessels for you.' She secretly left her sun-shield behind, went back to the spring, and asked the man to marry her; and thus she alone of all the women had a man for her husband, for all the rest had only tortoises. In due time she had a child; and when the other women discovered the secret, they paid the sisters to let them all marry the man, so that he had very many spouses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: After the man's first child had grown, he determined to leave the island; uncovering his canoe, he paddled away to his own home, where he saw the signs put up in the house of the dead, for all thought him drowned. It was evening when he reached his village, and as he rapped on the drum to let his wife know that he had returned, she called out, 'Who is there?' to which he answered, 'It is I.' She lit a torch and came out of the house and looked at him; but was angry, and saying, 'You are the one who caused us to spend all our bead-money in vain on your funeral ceremonies, while you have been living shamelessly with other wives,' she seized an axe and struck him so that he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tapa-Beater That Became a Woman

region.en: German New Guinea coast (symbolic pin: Huon Gulf)
region.zh: 德屬新幾內亞海岸（象徵定位：休恩灣）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A tapa-beater transformed itself into a woman, lured her bedfellow out night-fishing, and abandoned her on an island of driftwood. A sea-eagle hatched from an egg in her hand fed her, brought fire, and at last carried her home; her father burned the deceptive beater.
summary.zh: 夜裡，一根打布棒自化為女子之形，喚同屋女子：『起來，我們捕魚去。』二人秉炬出海，至漂流木之小島；天明，同伴現出打布棒原形，棄她而去。女子拾得海雕之卵，孵化育之；雕鳥捕魚奉食，並銜火枝予她炊食，終以巨木試力，攜她飛回本島。父母大喜，厚養雕鳥；父聞打布棒之詐，燃起大火，將棒投入焚之。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); New Guinea coast heritage.

passages.text: One night, while two women were sleeping in a house, a tapa-beater transformed itself into a woman resembling one of the pair, and waking the other, said to her, 'Come, it is time for us to go fishing.' So the woman arose, and they took torches and went out to sea in a canoe. After a while she saw an island of drift-wood, and as the dawn came on, perceived that her companion had turned into a tapa-beater, whereupon she said: 'Oh, the tapa-beater has deceived me. While we were talking in the evening, it was standing in the corner and heard us, and in the night it came and deceived me.' Landing her on the island, the tapa-beater paddled away and abandoned her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But she sought for food, and found a sea-eagle's egg which she held in her hand until it broke and hatched out a young bird, for which she cared until it grew large. Then the bird would fly off and get fish for her to eat, and also brought her a fire-brand, so that she could cook her food. When the bird said that he would carry her to the shore, she doubted whether he was strong enough; then the bird seized a great log of wood and showed her that he could lift that, so she trusted him and was borne safely back to her own island. Her father was angry at the tapa-beater's deception, and building a great fire, threw the tapa-beater into it and burned it up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ghost and His Own Corpse

region.en: Kai country, Huon Gulf, German New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 德屬新幾內亞休恩灣凱人之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A youngest brother fell from a tree and died; his ghost lied its way down, secretly wrapped and hid the body, and played the 'I forgot something' trick on the other brothers. The village shut its doors; only an old woman's door stood open, and the ghost bargained her grandson against his own corpse until dawn forced him to yield — and he became a wild tero-plant, his body a piece of bark.
summary.zh: 凱人兄弟爬樹採製臂環之料，幼弟失足墜亡；其鬼謊稱踏斷枯枝，先下樹裹屍藏之，途中屢以『忘了東西』為名回去搬屍，兄弟疑而逃歸，全村閉戶。唯老嫗與孫未聞警，門仍敞開。鬼擲屍入屋，老嫗擲出，鬼接而復擲；相持間老嫗誤將孫兒擲出，鬼大喜：『此可為我食矣！』天將曉，嫗呼日出，鬼懼日光，終以孫換屍，不再能隱，化為野特羅草，其屍則成一片樹皮。

passages.text: A number of brothers who were gathering material for making arm-bands had climbed into a great tree, when the youngest made a mis-step, and falling to the ground, was killed. The other brothers, who could not see what had happened because of the thick foliage, called out, 'What was that which fell?' The ghost of the dead brother, however, still stood in the tree and said, 'I stepped on a dead branch which broke,' and thus lying to his brothers, he descended from the tree before them, wrapped his body in leaves, and hid it. On the way back he repeated the trick of going back for 'something he had left' until his brothers, becoming suspicious, watched and found out how they had been deceived. Thereupon they all fled, and coming to the village, cried out, 'We have seen something mysterious. Shut your doors.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the ghost came, carrying his body on his back. He tried to throw his corpse into the first house, but it struck against the closed door and fell down again; so he picked it up and cast it at the next with like result. Thus he tried them all until he came to the last house, in which the old woman lived; and here, because the door was open, the ghost succeeded and threw his body into the house. Quickly the old woman seized the bundle and tossed it out again, but the ghost caught it and hurled it back. Thus they continued to send the body to and fro; but at last the old woman seized her grandson by mistake and threw him out, at which the ghost cried, 'That is great! Now you have given me something to eat.' The old woman then said, 'Throw him back again,' but the ghost replied, thinking to cheat her, 'Do you first throw out my body. Then I will throw him back.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they argued until dawn was near, when the old woman shouted, 'The dawn is coming. Does that mean something for you or for me?' Since the ghost replied, 'For me!' the woman delayed until the day had come. The light of the sun put the ghost in danger, so he threw the grandson back and received his own body in return; but being no longer able to conceal himself, he was changed into a wild tero-plant, while his body became a piece of bark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Rat Got His Tail and the Rail His Red Brow
title.zh: 鼠尾與紅額秧雞之由來

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A rat and a rail quarrelled over a gariga-fruit tree. The rat ate all the ripe fruit and threw down only stones; one struck the rail on the forehead and stuck there — the rail's red brow. Coming down, the rat was jabbed with a dracaena leaf that stuck fast in his rump: his tail.
summary.zh: 鼠與秧雞爭爬一樹，鼠食盡熟果，只擲石下來。秧雞誘其擲一枚，石果正中其額黏住——秧雞之紅額由此而來。鼠下樹時，秧雞以龍血樹葉插其臀，葉黏不去——鼠尾便是那片龍血樹葉。

passages.text: In the Banks Islands it is said that a rat and a rail, once finding a gariga-tree full of ripe fruit, disputed which should climb the tree. At last the rat went up, but instead of throwing ripe fruit down to the rail, he ate them himself and tossed down only stones. Finding that the rat refused to give him any fully ripe fruit, the bird said, 'Throw me down that one. It is only red ripe,' whereupon the rat took the fruit and tossed it at the rail, so that it hit him on his forehead and stuck fast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: The rail was angry, and as the rat came down from the tree, he thrust the unfolded leaf of a dracaena into the rat's rump, where it stuck fast. So the tail of the rat is the leaf of the dracaena that the rail put there, and the red lump on the head of the rail is the gariga-fruit which the rat threw at him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yam That Ate a Chicken

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: A wild yam rose up and devoured one of a hen's ten chickens; the survivors took shelter under a kite, which seized the man-eating yam and dropped it, and a second kite split it in two. The two halves fell to the two kites — whence some yams are good and some are bad.
summary.zh: 麻瘋島上，一母雞率十雛遇野薯，薯起身吞食一雛。倖存者呼鳶庇護，藏於其翼下；野薯質問，鳶怒而抓薯高飛擲地，另一鳶再抓再擲，薯裂為二——兩鳶分而食之，故今之薯有好有壞。

passages.text: In Lepers Island in the New Hebrides the origin of good and bad yams is given as follows. One day a hen and her ten chickens came across a wild yam, which got up after a while and ate one of the chickens. The survivors called to a kite, which said to the hen, 'Put the chickens under me,' and when the yam came and asked the kite where the chickens were, the bird replied, 'I don't know.' Thereupon the yam scolded the kite, and the latter, seizing the yam, flew high into the air and dropped it to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then another kite took it up and let it fall from a great height, so that the yam was broken into two parts; and thus the two kites divided the yam between them and ate it, whence some yams are good for food and some are bad — the garden patch carrying to this day the memory of the chicken-eating wild yam and the two birds that broke it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Turtle Got His Shell

region.en: British New Guinea coast (symbolic pin: Port Moresby)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞海岸（象徵定位：莫爾茲比港）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The turtle and the wallaby raided Binama the hornbill's garden. The wallaby leapt away; the turtle was caught for the morrow's feast, bribed Binama's children with games and finery, and plunged into the sea wearing a great wooden bowl — which the stones of the pursuing birds could not break. To this day all turtles carry the bowl of Binama's house on their backs.
summary.zh: 龜與袋鼠同入犀鳥比納馬之園偷食蕉蔗。袋鼠一躍而逃，龜被縛於架上以待翌日宴殺。龜哄比納馬之子女解縛同戲，戴上珠串、貝釧，背上負一大木碗，趁眾人歸而奔海。眾人追至岸邊擲石，擊碎雙釧與珠串，木碗卻堅不可破；龜遂遠遁。至今龜背所負，即是比納馬家中之木碗。

passages.text: The turtle and the wallaby, being hungry one day, went together to the hornbill's garden and began to eat his bananas and sugar-cane. While they were thus engaged, the birds were preparing a feast, and Binama, the hornbill, asked one of them to go to the shore for some salt water with which to flavour the food; the wagtail agreed to go, and on the way passed through Binama's garden, where he saw the wallaby and the turtle feasting. The wagtail returned to the village by another path and cried out, 'Friends, the turtle and the wallaby are eating in our master's garden.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then all the people were angry, and getting their spears, they ran and surrounded the garden. The wallaby, seeing his danger, made a tremendous leap and escaped, but the turtle, having no means of flight, was caught and carried prisoner to Binama's house, where he was tied to a pole and laid upon a shelf until the morrow, when Binama and the others intended to kill the turtle at a feast. Only Binama's children were left in the house, and the turtle, speaking softly to them, said, 'Loosen my bonds, O children, that we may play together.' This the children did, and at the turtle's request got the best of their father's ornaments, which the turtle donned: a great bead necklace, shell armlets, and a huge wooden bowl on his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the people could be heard returning; and as soon as the turtle became aware of this, he ran swiftly to the sea and dived out of sight. The birds hurled great stones at him and broke one of the armlets, then the other, and hit the necklace so that the string gave way and the beads were lost. Then for a last time calling to the turtle to show himself, they threw very large stones which fell upon the wooden bowl on his back, but they did not break it, and the turtle was not harmed. Then he fled far away over the sea, and to this day all turtles carry on their backs the bowl that once was in the house of Binama.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dog, the Kangaroo, and the Broken Forepaws

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. III

summary.en: The kangaroo tricked the dog into eating filth for a yellow lafua-fruit; the dog repaid him by boasting of his own broken forepaws until the kangaroo snapped his off — then killed the maimed trickster. Ever since, the kangaroo has had short forepaws.
summary.zh: 袋鼠食黃色拉富阿果，狗問其口何以黃；袋鼠指穢物謊稱即是，狗食之受騙。狗懷恨，先埋掌於沙，謊稱自斷前掌故而短美，誘袋鼠效之；袋鼠自斷雙掌，狗躍起曰：『我掌仍在！是你騙我食穢。』撲而殺之。袋鼠短掌之形，自此而傳。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage. Dixon notes close parallels with Australian tales.

passages.text: One day when the kangaroo was going along, followed by the dog, he ate a yellow lafua-fruit and was asked by the dog, when the latter came up with him, 'Tell me, what have you eaten that your mouth is so yellow?' The kangaroo replied, 'There is some of it on yonder log,' pointing to a pile of filth; whereupon the dog, thinking that it was good, ran quickly and ate it up, only to hear his companion laugh and say, 'Listen, friend, what I ate was a yellow lafua-fruit like that; what you have eaten is simply filth.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Angered at the trick played upon him, the dog resolved to have his revenge, and so, as they went on toward the shore, he ran ahead and buried his forepaws in the sand. When the kangaroo came up, the dog said: 'Gracious, but you have long forepaws! Break off a piece of your long paws. I have broken off a piece of mine as you see, and now mine are beautiful and short. Do you do likewise, and then we shall both be alike.' So the kangaroo broke off a piece of each of his forepaws and threw the pieces away, whereupon the dog jumped up and said, triumphantly, 'Aha! I still have long forepaws, but you have only short ones. You are the one who deceived me and made me eat the filth,' and as he uttered these words, he sprang at the kangaroo and killed him, and ever since the kangaroo has had short forepaws.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. III (1916); not verbatim.
